The Hell You Say, The new battles over free speech are fierce, but who is censoring whom?

A rather interesting piece, though I'm not without a measure of criticism toward it. It all concludes with the question of protecting online speech on private platforms, questioning whose speech is being protected. At present, there is a legal notion that the company in the middle engages in speech via the actions of their users. I find this notion to be entirely absurd. The same company that utilizes it's supposed right to free speech as a tool of blatant censorship and social control will in turn refuse to accept liability for the actual content of it's userbase's speech. Why is that? Is the user's speech not the company's speech? They claim that it is their speech and not the speech of the user when it suits their interests, yet they claim the exact opposite the moment you attach hazard toward their claimed actions. How can a website or any other platform use free speech as a justification to censor others, a justification that hinges on the notion that it is the platform's speech possibly exist when that platform is not willing to accept the full consequences, without immunity or reduction when that speech is retracted?

I hold that they can not utilize free speech as such a justification, given their unwillingness to take responsibility for all of their supposed speech. It is an act of cowardice perpetuated by petty tyrants seeking to carve out their own private kingdom in which only some ideas are permitted to exist. A TV station, a radio broadcast, a website... These are not individuals with points of view being forced to speak against their will. They are mere conduits through which speech is transmitted. Do your telephone lines have the special right of free speech that might silence your words whenever you wish to speak? Does the very air? As conduits of information, they serve not as participants but as simple infrastructure. They are the road upon which speech drives. A road has no speech rights to deny access to cars painted red on Saturdays, why should any other basic infrastructure be allowed to make such a claim? The very notion is absurd.

That said, I will return toward the beginning and the story of that maligned DJ. I do not agree with the girl that raised a dispute with him and then the club. I think it was in poor taste. While I can understand why someone might feel that way about the matter, I have also known women that play hard to get with full intention toward the suggested outcome from the start. Whether or not such a thing equates to a culture of rape hinges entirely upon the subjective experience of the people within the story. Absent the fullness of a real scene, we must fill in the blanks with our imaginations. We make assumptions about what might and might not be occurring. Were the situation less ambiguous, I would likely side with the complaining girl, but that's not what was happening. Even though I disagree, I do think it was up to the individuals there at the time to come up with their own solution to the dilemma. The business made a choice to satisfy an unreasonable customer rather than cause a scene. I can understand why they would do that, even if it's incredibly unfair to the person that was just trying to make a living.

I think it's fair that people criticized him on social media, just as I think it's fair that her online reputation was devastated as a result of her unreasonable behavior. When we engage in social interaction with one another, we assume certain risks. These risks are not violent but they exist. You can neither expect nor force someone to like you. No matter your views, no matter how right or wrong you are there will always be some who agree with you and some who disagree. These disagreements are a fundamental aspect of human existence. Rather than seeking to diminish the experience of our humanity by squashing troublesome viewpoints, we should engage with one another on equal levels. We should argue, discuss, exchange points of view. We should cite factual sources, conduct research along the lines of our assertions. We should also consider the opposing viewpoints we face, performing equal research into their own perspective.

It is through such disagreement that we gain opportunity to learn, to grow. We become exposed to new ideas, new world views. We express ourselves in all of our unavoidable imperfections. You can not kill free speech through private or even public disagreement. You are not engaging in censorship when you refuse to participate in a business transaction that will profit those you perceive to be actively harming you. If a business is engaged in political actions with which you disagree then you are speaking the language of that business when you refuse to give it your patronage. That business will understand that you object to their ways and will have to decide whether it places more value on social inclusion or it's present position. That is the central idea behind the notion "vote with your wallet." Unfortunately, politics has become polarized to the point that everyone divides into broad camps seeking to destroy one another outright. One side will offend. The other side responds with an embargo. The other side pours resources in to the besieged business in an attempt to defeat their opponent's speech. Both sides begin to claim status as martyrs, screaming of how the other side is abusing them beyond all measure and reason. It makes for the most ridiculous drama known to man.

This self-victimization serves no purpose. The issue is not the speech, the offense or commonplace social responses to disliked speech. The problem is that people have forgotten what it is to disagree, forgotten that while there are differences there are also points of common interest. We divide into tribes, attack one another based on superficial identity politics and are in turn attacked by the superficial presumptions of the uncoordinated masses. What purpose does this social warfare serve? Does it enrich our lives in any way? Do we gain greater insights when we insist upon divided echo chambers that infinitely reinforce our own confirmation bias? I can not see the benefit to that approach, if one even exists.

I assert that we humans are all afraid of each other in varying degrees. We form instinctive tribal bonds with those perceived as similar, banding together against those that differ through our instinctive notion of mutual self-protection. This is a mistake. The other side isn't an enemy, the other side is a potential ally that might see some of your own reason if you only stop to speak with one another in a manner that allows understanding to take root.

Take the divide between religious conservatives and the gay community as one example. Both sides have strongly held personal convictions, both sides believe in absolute terms that their views are correct, that the other side is seeking to destroy them. Both sides are motivated from fear of the other, both seek to preempt the actions of the other group in order to maintain enough of a strategic advantage to feel comfortable, safe. Strip away all the fighting, all the bullshit, let them see each other for what they really are without prejudice getting in the way. The religious conservatives would come to understand that many gay people are living upstanding and virtuous lives by any moral standard that exists, except for the gay sex part. The gays would see people that are merely confused about them, that don't understand. It is possible to create that understanding, for the religious conservatives to realize that the gays aren't trying to destroy their faith or religion, to turn all the world gay. Then in the absence of political constraints against the gay community, does it really matter to them if the religious conservatives hold a different belief set? I don't think it matters, not really.

Only by arguing, exchanging ideas can we get to know one another and only by getting to know one another can we dispel the ignorance that perpetually cripples the rate of human progress throughout history.

That's fine in principle, but the thick curtain that hid the capitalist elite so well for the last two hundred years is growing rather thin under constant criticism and investigation thanks to the internet. Distribution of wealth is a major concern, and when the list of people with enough money to establish successful large scale media operations is absurdly small, it's little wonder that we're left with polarizing news that panders to agendas -- mainly, feeding the populace with the exact formulation of stockholder views that will drive their profits and keep the handful of elite firmly in control.

Compartmentalization has given the population more freedom than ever to choose which slave master he will serve for the rest of his days. Spreading ideas is expensive, therefor people with deeper pockets can get their ideas spread most effectively. They choose to spread ideas that give them the best return on investment, or convince the population to elect a candidate that serves their interests. We can at least see a little behind the curtain now, get some idea for the shell game they've been subjecting us to for a long time now. You make good points. I am with you on the distribution issue. I'm sticking with break up the media. Our information stream is clogged. There is no satisfactory workaround -- although we should also continue trying. Break it up. Then, we can at least get more information on the distribution issue and every other issue.

I really don't think we need to break up the media, it would suffice if the public simply ignored them in favor of independent journalists. Rags like the New Yorker are fairly obliged to set money before liberty because their subscribers are all gone, the same with the rest of the newspapers and periodicals. We all get our news online for free... Yet they stay in business. How? That question turns my attention toward the rise of adverjournalism, with paid articles masquerading as legitimate unbiased news. Every time we turn to the media or rely on the media, we're counting on the corporate propaganda mill. We should figure out a way to set up and support impartial independent journalism instead of finding a way to break the existing problem into a larger number of slightly smaller problems.

We don't need big stations with studios. Recording and broadcast equipment is cheap, and it's everywhere. It's easy to use, it works across our global communications network in real time and costs virtually nothing if you're already connected. I feel like we can do a lot more by supporting outfits like VICE News than bitching about the latest CNN shillery. There's still real news out there, you just have to go looking for it because you won't find it on the TV.
